name: Sentinel-2 20 m to 10 m super-resolution as preprocessing

identity.method_name: DSen2 / VDSen2 CNN super-resolution, and 2025 channel-attention + high-frequency-enhancement variants, applied as a 20 m to 10 m sharpening step for Sentinel-2 B11 (SWIR) before MNDWI computation
identity.core_idea: DSen2 is a residual CNN trained (via synthetic downsampling of real 10 m bands, since no true 10 m ground truth exists for the 20 m/60 m bands) to predict what the 20 m bands (B05, B06, B07, B8A, B11, B12) would look like at 10 m, using the native 10 m bands (B02, B03, B04, B08) as high-resolution spatial guidance. VDSen2 is the same idea with a deeper (66-layer) network. 2025 variants add a channel-attention block (to weight bands by how much they benefit from sharpening) and a high-pass-frequency enhancement branch (to recover edge detail specifically) on top of the DSen2 backbone. Applied here, the point is to sharpen B11 to 10 m before computing MNDWI = (Green - SWIR)/(Green + SWIR), so the index's two inputs share a common 10 m grid instead of forcing Green down to 20 m, in principle giving crisper shorelines, especially for small lakes.
identity.official_dataset_ids: None as a data product -- this is a model architecture applied at inference time. Code: github.com/lanha/DSen2. Input remains the project's existing COPERNICUS Sentinel-2 L2A source via Earth Search STAC (tile 43PGQ), but would require pulling additional 20 m bands (B05, B06, B07, B8A, B12) that the project's current band list (B02, B03, B04, B08, B11, SCL) does not include, since DSen2 needs the full 20 m/10 m band complement to run its joint model, not B11 alone.

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Not applicable in the encroachment-labelling sense -- this is a preprocessing filter, not a classifier or detector. The strategy for the sharpening model itself is self-supervised: DSen2's own weights were learned by synthetically downsampling real 10 m bands and training the network to reverse that degradation (the 'Wald protocol' assumption that the same downsampling relationship holds at native 20 m -> 10 m). No true 10 m ground truth for B11 exists anywhere, in this project or in the original DSen2 paper, so any performance claim about the sharpened B11 is itself only ever validated indirectly (see evaluation).
fit_to_project.input_required: Full Sentinel-2 L1C or L2A tile with all 10 m bands (B02, B03, B04, B08) and the target 20 m bands (B05, B06, B07, B8A, B11, B12), plus DSen2's pretrained weights. The project currently only pulls B02, B03, B04, B08, B11 and SCL, so B05, B06, B07, B8A and B12 would need to be additionally fetched from Earth Search STAC for each of the 42 lake-years -- a small but real extra acquisition step, not a re-use of existing data.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: Not applicable as a per-lake-year sample-size question -- DSen2 is not trained on this project's data at all; it runs pretrained, per-pixel, per-scene. Reframed at the pixel level it operates on all ~900,000 pixels of each of the 42 scenes (network inference only, no fitting), so there is no small-sample training constraint here, only an inference cost (trivial) and a domain-shift risk (the network was never trained on Indian urban lake/wetland scenes specifically).
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: yes -- it needs no lake-specific labels or ground truth to run, since it uses publicly released pretrained weights trained on globally distributed scenes with a self-supervised (synthetic downsampling) objective.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: This is exactly the resolution problem the method targets: B11 is native 20 m and the project's current pipeline resamples everything (including the native-10 m bands B02/B03/B04/B08) down onto a common 20 m grid, discarding the resolution advantage those bands actually have. Applying DSen2 would invert that: B11 gets sharpened up to 10 m and the project's working grid would need to move to 10 m instead of being downsampled to 20 m -- a genuine architecture change to the existing pipeline, not a drop-in add-on, and it directly targets the smallest lakes: Sankey Tank at 12.4 ha is only about 310 pixels at 20 m (confirmed: 12.4 ha = 124,000 sq m / 400 sq m per 20 m pixel = 310 pixels) but would be roughly 1,240 pixels at 10 m, a fourfold increase in boundary-pixel resolution.
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: None -- self-supervised pretrained network, no manual labelling required.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: None of the project's four stated limitations. It does not add rows (limitation 1), does not touch the OpenStreetMap building snapshot problem (limitation 2), does not create or substitute for ground truth (limitation 3), and does not add temporal frequency -- it still produces exactly one sharpened scene per lake per year, so the dry-season-only sampling problem (limitation 4) is completely unaffected. This is a spatial-resolution fix layered on top of a project whose four documented problems are all sample-size, labelling, and temporal-frequency problems, not spatial-resolution problems -- so it is orthogonal to, not curative of, any of them.
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: No. Sharpening the SWIR band changes how precisely a shoreline is drawn on a given date; it says nothing about why the water extent changed between dates. Bellandur's desilting-driven collapse from 15.7 ha (2019) to 0.4 ha (2021) back to 107.9 ha (2025) would be reproduced, just at a sharper spatial resolution, with the same ambiguity about cause.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: No, and it could subtly interact with it: hyacinth mats classify as vegetation via NDVI regardless of how precisely B11 is resolved, since the confound is spectral (mat canopy reflects like vegetation), not a resolution artefact. A super-resolved B11 could, if anything, sharpen the false boundary between water and hyacinth mat with more apparent (but not more true) confidence, which is a subtle risk worth flagging rather than a benefit.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None. The sharpened shoreline still only maps to the OpenStreetMap proxy polygon; no buffer distance (30 m Master Plan, 75 m NGT, KTCDA record) is being tested or made traceable by improving pixel resolution.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: Unaffected -- sharpening is applied independently, per band, per scene; it does not add or interpolate additional acquisition dates. It is a purely spatial, not temporal, intervention.

implementation.libraries: Original DSen2 (github.com/lanha/DSen2): TensorFlow/Keras, written against an older TensorFlow 1.x-era API -- expect dependency friction on a modern Python/TensorFlow 2.x setup and likely a need to pin an old TF version or run inside a compatibility shim/Docker container. No public code repository was found for the 2025 channel-attention + high-frequency-enhancement variant (the Frontiers 2025 paper's data-availability statement points only to a Google Drive dataset link, not a code release), so the practical, actually-runnable option today is the original DSen2/VDSen2, not the newer variant. [verify]
implementation.pretrained_weights: DSen2 provides pretrained weights trained on 60 globally distributed Sentinel-2 tiles (diverse biomes/climate zones), derived from Sentinel-2 L1C top-of-atmosphere reflectance via synthetic downsampling; these can be used directly for inference on new tiles without retraining. The project's imagery is L2A surface reflectance, so band scaling/offset conventions (the project's DN * 0.0001 - 0.1 convention under processing baseline 04.00+) would need to be reconciled with whatever normalisation DSen2's weights expect -- a real but manageable integration detail, not a blocker.
implementation.licence: DSen2 code is GPL-3.0. Usable in an academic capstone project without issue, but note (for completeness) that GPL-3.0 requires any distributed derivative code to also be released under GPL-3.0 -- not a concern for a non-distributed student project, but worth stating since it is the one licence flag in this pipeline.
implementation.compute_requirement: CPU-feasible for inference at this project's scale (42 scenes of ~900,000 pixels each); no training is required if using the released pretrained weights, so this fits comfortably within free Colab/Kaggle GPU limits or even a laptop CPU, taking at most minutes per scene.
implementation.student_days: About 1-2 days to get the older DSen2 TensorFlow environment running (likely the main friction point) and fetch the additional 20 m bands (B05/B06/B07/B8A/B12) not currently in the pipeline, plus 1 day to run inference across all 42 scenes and re-derive MNDWI at 10 m, plus 1 day to run and report the Wald-protocol self-consistency check needed to say anything evidence-based about whether it helped. Roughly 3-4 student-days total for a preprocessing add-on.

evaluation.metrics: Since there is no true 10 m ground truth for B11 anywhere (this project or the literature), the method cannot be judged by shoreline accuracy against a real reference. It should instead be judged by: (1) the Wald-protocol self-consistency RMSE/SSIM (see validation_protocol), and (2) a before/after comparison of the derived quantity that actually matters to the project -- water-area pixel count and shoreline perimeter for each lake, especially the small ones (Sankey Tank) -- reported as a sensitivity check, not as an accuracy claim.
evaluation.validation_protocol: Not a leave-one-lake-out / temporal-hold-out situation, because this step is not fit to the project's own labelled outcome at all -- it is an unsupervised preprocessing filter. The correct and only available validation is the Wald protocol used in the super-resolution literature itself: take the project's own real 10 m bands, synthetically downsample them to 20 m, run them back through the sharpening network, and compare the reconstruction to the known original 10 m values (RMSE, SSIM, spectral angle). This validates the network's general sharpening behaviour on the project's actual scenes, but it can never directly validate the one thing that matters here -- whether the specific B11 sharpening at each lake's true native 20 m resolution is accurate -- because that 10 m truth for B11 does not exist to check against.
evaluation.leakage_risk: Minimal for the sharpening step itself, since it is not trained or fit on the project's data (pretrained weights only) -- so there is no train/test leakage of lake identity in the usual sense. The residual risk is domain-shift, not leakage: the network's pretrained weights were learned on globally diverse land cover, not specifically on Indian urban wetland/hyacinth-choked lake edges, so its learned sharpening prior may not transfer cleanly to this specific scene type, and there is no way to detect that failure without exactly the ground truth the project lacks.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: None from the network itself -- DSen2 and its variants output a single point-estimate sharpened image with no confidence map or calibrated interval. Any uncertainty statement here would have to be constructed externally (e.g., the spread between DSen2 and a simple bicubic/pan-sharpening baseline as a bracket), and even that is an ad hoc, not a calibrated, interval.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Not applicable in the SMOTE/GAN/tabular-augmentation sense -- no synthetic project data is generated here. There is, however, an analogous and real risk worth disclosing: CNN super-resolution can hallucinate spatial detail that looks sharper without being more true (texture invented from correlated 10 m bands rather than measured in B11 itself), which could produce a shoreline that appears more precise while being no more accurate, or even systematically biased at ambiguous water/hyacinth edges. If this method is used, that risk should be stated alongside any 'improved shoreline' claim, exactly as an augmentation risk would be.

evidence.published_performance: DSen2 original (Lanaras, Bioucas-Dias, Galliani, Baltsavias & Schindler, 2018, ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing 146:305-319, doi:10.1016/j.isprsjprs.2018.09.018; arXiv:1803.04271): reports roughly a 50% RMSE reduction versus bicubic interpolation for 2x (20 m -> 10 m) upsampling on their held-out test tiles, but with markedly weaker performance specifically on B8A, B11 and B12 (RMSE figures exceeding 38 reflectance-scale units reported in follow-on comparative work) [verify -- exact original-paper RMSE units and per-band table not independently re-confirmed from primary text in this pass]. The 2025 channel-attention + high-frequency-enhancement variant (Nguyen-Vi, Bui-Quoc & Kamel, Frontiers in Remote Sensing, 2025, doi:10.3389/frsen.2025.1644460) reports B11 RMSE improving from 39.80 (DSen2 baseline, their re-run) to 38.00 (proposed method) on their own 2x-upsampling test set -- a roughly 4.5% relative reduction in B11 error, the exact band this method needs for MNDWI. [verify] Neither paper reports any water-index, shoreline, or MNDWI-specific evaluation -- both are evaluated purely on generic image reconstruction error (RMSE per band), so the specific downstream claim this project would need ('does sharpened B11 improve the water mask') has not actually been demonstrated in either source and would need to be established independently.
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: DSen2: 60 globally distributed Sentinel-2 tiles spanning diverse biomes and climate zones (45 for training/validation, 15 held out for testing), no lake- or wetland-specific sites. The 2025 CA+HPF variant: 30 regions across Vietnam plus 9 held-out test regions, again general land-cover scenes, not water bodies. Neither work's reported numbers were obtained on urban lake shorelines or anything resembling this project's 6 Bengaluru lakes, so their RMSE figures are evidence of general sharpening capability, not of shoreline-mask improvement at this project's scale.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No direct application to Indian lakes or Bengaluru specifically was found for DSen2, VDSen2, or the 2025 variant. The closest conceptually related (but non-deep-learning) precedent is Du, Zhang, Ling, Weng, Feng & Zhang (2016), 'Water Bodies' Mapping from Sentinel-2 Imagery with Modified Normalized Difference Water Index at 10-m Spatial Resolution Produced by Sharpening the SWIR Band', MDPI Remote Sensing 8(4):354, doi:10.3390/rs8040354, which sharpens SWIR to 10 m using a regression-based (not CNN) pan-sharpening approach specifically to improve MNDWI, tested on water bodies in China -- not India, and not deep learning, but the only source found that validates the same downstream idea (sharpened SWIR -> better MNDWI) that this method proposes. [verify]
evidence.evidence_recency: 2025 (Frontiers CA+HPF variant) is the newest and most relevant architecture; the only publicly runnable implementation with released pretrained weights remains DSen2 from 2018, which is pre-2020 -- flagged accordingly, since the practical version of this method a student could actually deploy rests on 2018-era code and weights, not the state-of-the-art 2025 architecture.
evidence.primary_sources: DSen2: Lanaras et al. 2018, doi:10.1016/j.isprsjprs.2018.09.018; arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.04271; code https://github.com/lanha/DSen2. VDSen2 (very-deep variant, same paper). 2025 channel-attention + high-frequency-enhancement variant: Frontiers in Remote Sensing, doi:10.3389/frsen.2025.1644460, https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/remote-sensing/articles/10.3389/frsen.2025.1644460/full. Fast shallow-CNN alternative: Palsson et al., 'Fast Super-Resolution of 20 m Sentinel-2 Bands Using Convolutional Neural Networks', MDPI Remote Sensing 11(22):2635, https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/11/22/2635. Spectral-attention precursor (2022): MDPI Remote Sensing 14(12):2890, doi:10.3390/rs14122890. SWIR-sharpening-for-MNDWI precedent (non-DL): Du et al. 2016, doi:10.3390/rs8040354.

risk.failure_modes: Domain shift: pretrained weights learned on generic global land cover may hallucinate or blur texture at water/hyacinth-mat boundaries specific to Indian urban wetlands, a scene type absent from the training data of either DSen2 or the 2025 variant. Integration risk: the older DSen2 codebase's TensorFlow-version dependencies can consume disproportionate setup time relative to the benefit. Band-availability risk: the project would need to fetch and store additional 20 m bands (B05/B06/B07/B8A/B12) it does not currently use, adding pipeline complexity for a method that only changes one of those bands' resolution (B11). Most importantly, the method does not touch either of this project's two central analytical problems (desilting, hyacinth) -- it only sharpens pixels, so the payoff is confined to boundary precision on the smallest lakes.
risk.panel_defensibility: A panel will ask 'how do you know the sharpened edge is more correct, not just sharper-looking?' -- the only honest answer is the Wald-protocol self-consistency check (synthetic downsample-and-reconstruct RMSE/SSIM on the project's own imagery), since no true 10 m SWIR reference exists to check against directly; without running and reporting that check, any 'improved shoreline' claim is unverifiable and should not be presented as a result. A second likely question -- 'did this change your actual encroachment finding for any lake?' -- requires a concrete before/after area comparison, especially for Sankey Tank, to justify the added pipeline complexity at all.
risk.honest_expectation: At best, a modest, verifiable-in-principle increase in boundary-pixel count and shoreline smoothness for the smallest lakes (Sankey Tank, and possibly Kaikondrahalli), with negligible practical effect on the larger, already pixel-rich lakes (Bellandur, Varthur). It is very unlikely to change the qualitative encroachment conclusion for any lake, and it does nothing for the desilting or hyacinth confounds, which remain the project's real analytical bottleneck. A defensible framing is: 'we tested it as an optional sensitivity check for the smallest lake and it made [no material / a small, quantified] difference to the water-area estimate' -- a null or marginal result here is entirely plausible and should be reported as such rather than oversold.

verdict.recommended_rank: adopt-if-time -- worth running once as a documented sensitivity check specifically for Sankey Tank (and any other sub-20-ha lake) given the direct 4x pixel-count argument, but not worth building into the core pipeline as a required preprocessing step, since it addresses none of the project's four stated limitations or its two central confounds, and its own literature has never validated the specific downstream claim (shoreline/MNDWI improvement) this project would be relying on.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: I tested whether super-resolving the SWIR band to 10 m before computing MNDWI changes the water-mask area for the smallest lake, Sankey Tank, validating the sharpening step only with the standard synthetic-downsampling self-consistency check since no true 10 m SWIR ground truth exists anywhere; it is included as an optional, disclosed sensitivity check rather than part of the primary pipeline, since it does not address the project's core desilting/hyacinth/sample-size problems.
